content.p: Carl Anthony Williams was a high-school dropout and amphetamine dealer from Melbourne's north who became, in the ABC's words, the most notorious figure of what it called Australia's longest-running and deadliest gangland war. He was convicted of ordering the murders of four rivals and of conspiring to kill a fifth, and in May 2007 a Supreme Court judge sentenced him to life with a minimum of 35 years. He called himself "The Premier". Justice Betty King, sentencing him, said he had employed others to do the actual killing.

Three years later, on 19 April 2010 another prisoner clubbed him to death in the supposedly secure Acacia unit of Barwon Prison. His death collapsed a murder prosecution that he had helped build, set off an Ombudsman's inquiry, and is still described by a former senior police officer as a planned killing in which people have never been held to account.

Williams was born on 13 October 1970 and attended Broadmeadows West Technical School, leaving in year 11. By 1999 he was dealing amphetamines. On 13 October of that year, his 29th birthday, he was shot in the stomach. The ABC stated that Jason Moran shot him and The Age said he did so allegedly; CNN reported that the Moran brothers "allegedly" did it, and a Sydney Morning Herald columnist wrote that Jason Moran did it in the company of his half-brother Mark.

The accounts of the quarrel behind it overlap but are not identical. CNN said the Morans accused Williams of undercutting them by selling cheap pills. The ABC said the argument was over money and an ecstasy pill-pressing machine. The Herald columnist added a drug debt of $400,000 and said Williams's future wife, Roberta, had left a Moran associate to live with him. Williams himself later called the shooting the catalyst of the war.

Police said the two families had both trafficked drugs in Melbourne for years and had once been associates. Drug charges followed within weeks. On 25 November that year he, his father George and another man were charged after police raided an alleged amphetamine factory in Broadmeadows, where, a court later heard, officers seized between 25,000 and 30,000 tablets valued at up to $20 million.

CNN reported that Mark Moran was shot outside his home while taking out the rubbish eight months after the birthday shooting. On 21 June 2003 Jason Moran and an associate, Pasquale Barbaro, were shot dead in a van at a children's football clinic, with five children in the back seats. CNN called it the most horrific of the gangland murders. The Age's 2010 report gave the date of Jason Moran's murder as June 2000, which conflicts with the ABC and the Bendigo Advertiser, both of which give 21 June 2003. At Jason's funeral his mother, Judy, leaned over the coffin and said "all will be dealt with my darling".

The ABC's chronology records the other killings that Williams was later convicted of ordering: the charred body of Mark Mallia was found on 18 August 2003; Michael Marshall was shot outside his South Yarra home on 25 October 2003; and Lewis Moran was shot in an inner-suburban hotel on 31 March 2004. Days earlier, on 23 March 2004, Williams's friend and bodyguard Andrew Veniamin had been shot dead in a Carlton restaurant. Williams was a pallbearer at the funeral. Two days after the shooting he had said, "If anyone wants to come and get me, then come and get me - just don't miss."

The counts of the dead differ. The ABC wrote that the war ran from 1998 to 2006 and left 27 dead. CNN, writing in 2009, said 30 people had been killed over nine years. Police said Williams was linked to at least 10 underworld murders. Williams himself claimed in prison letters that he had never killed or harmed an innocent person, and that he had acted in defence of himself and his family.

In 2003 Victoria Police's chief commissioner, Christine Nixon, set up the Purana task force to investigate the murders. By June 2004 the ABC reported 27 execution-style killings in six years and only five men charged, over three of them. Williams was by then a notorious figure. Nixon banned him from Crown Casino on 2 April 2004, and in May the police used a rarely used provision about people of "notoriously bad character" to bar him from bars and clubs in the eight eastern suburbs covered by Stonnington City Council. Williams claimed, through an intermediary, that corrupt police were trying to have him killed.

On 9 June 2004 police arrested him at his mother's house in Brunswick in the early morning and charged him with conspiracy to murder and incitement to murder. A 16-year-old youth was also charged and two other men armed with a gun were arrested in Brighton, where a handgun was seized. About 150 officers took part in raids across the city. Assistant Commissioner Simon Overland called the arrests significant but said whether they proved to be "the turning point" was something only time would tell. Police did not name the intended victim, saying people's lives could be at stake.

Williams was sentenced to seven years for drug trafficking on 29 October 2004. In 2007 he pleaded guilty to murdering Jason Moran, Lewis Moran and Mark Mallia and to conspiring to murder Mario Condello; he had earlier been found guilty of killing Marshall. CNN's wording is that he pleaded guilty to four murders; The Age and the ABC give three murders and the conspiracy. The ABC's chronology lists the 35-year sentence for Lewis Moran, Jason Moran and Mallia, while The Age and the Bendigo Advertiser say it covered four murders and the Condello conspiracy. Justice Betty King told him there were "no other appropriate penalties for crimes of this nature". "You are a killer and a cowardly one who employed others to do the actual killing," she said. The Bendigo Advertiser's report adds that Condello was later shot dead in 2006.

In letters to his mother Barbara after sentencing, Williams wrote: "Yes, I did what I did, and nothing I or anyone does will ever change that." In the same letters he said he was proud of the person he saw in the mirror, complained that people whose crimes were as bad as his had got away lightly in exchange for his liberty, and objected to his portrayal in the television series Underbelly, saying it painted him as brain-dead.

Barbara Williams was found dead in her Essendon home on 22 November 2008. Police said an empty pill bottle lay beside her bed and the death was not being treated as suspicious; she was believed to have taken an overdose. Detective Senior Sergeant Ron Iddles said she had been suffering severe depression for 12 months. Her husband George was serving time for trafficking, and Carl was in jail. Williams was refused permission to attend her funeral, having been deemed too much of a flight risk, though a tribute from him was read out.

On the morning of 19 April 2010, a newspaper reported that Victoria Police had paid the fees for Williams's nine-year-old daughter to attend an exclusive private school. His lawyer, Rob Stary, said Williams was upset because the story put his daughter at risk. Shortly before 1pm, in the Acacia unit, another inmate, Matthew Johnson, crept up behind Williams while he sat in a common area and struck him on the head with the stem of an exercise bike. Williams suffered severe head injuries, went into cardiac arrest, and was pronounced dead at 1.47pm.

The first public accounts were confused. Police told reporters that two prisoners had attacked him, and The Age noted conflicting statements from police and Corrections officials about where it had happened. Deputy corrections commissioner Rod Wise said the three men in the unit were allowed together for six hours daily, from 8am to 2pm, without constant supervision, and that it was impractical to supervise every prisoner constantly. Stary countered that his client was in solitary confinement in the state's most secure environment, where every minute should have been supervised. Corrections Minister Bob Cameron announced three inquiries, by police, the coroner and the Office of Correctional Services Review.

Johnson, 38, a self-styled prison enforcer, pleaded not guilty. The ABC reported that CCTV showed him walking up behind Williams and striking him eight times, then dragging the body back to his cell, and that it took guards nearly 30 minutes to find Williams. At trial he admitted the killing but claimed self-defence: he said another prisoner, Tommy Ivanovic, had told him the day before that Williams planned to kill him with billiard balls in a sock. He told the jury he had intended to kill Williams and had hit him seven more times to make sure he was dead.

After a three-week trial in the Supreme Court and 14 hours of deliberation over three days, a jury of seven women and five men convicted him of murder in September 2011, rejecting both self-defence and defensive homicide. On 8 December 2011 Justice Lex Lasry sentenced him to life with a non-parole period of 32 years. He called Johnson's self-defence story "fanciful" and the crime appalling and the product of "some meaningless underworld prison code".

The judge's finding on motive tied the killing to Williams's co-operation. Williams had given police statements about the 2004 murders of the informer Terence Hodson and his wife Christine in their Kew home, implicating himself, the former detective Paul Dale and Rodney Collins. Dale and Collins had been charged. Johnson led a prisoners' group called the Prisoners of War, which despised anyone who helped police, and copies of Williams's statements were found on his computer, last opened two days before the killing. Justice Lasry said Williams's information was "pivotal" in implicating Dale and the accused hitman. Charges against Dale and Collins were withdrawn six weeks after Williams died. Dale has consistently maintained his innocence, and the ABC reports that a coronial inquest found the evidence insufficient to conclude he was behind the Hodsons' deaths.

Johnson had more than 150 prior convictions according to the ABC; a VICE writer put the figure at 167. VICE reported that his only words in his first police interview were "I acted alone". In December 2021 the ABC reported that he had filed an appeal against his conviction in the Victorian Court of Appeal, with a directions hearing set for the next day, and that he maintains his innocence. The ABC's report gave no outcome for the appeal.

Justice Lasry questioned why prison authorities had housed the two men together when Johnson posed a real threat to Williams. The ABC reported that a Victorian Ombudsman's report, released in April 2012, found that Justice Department secretary Penny Armytage had been repeatedly warned that Williams could be killed by a fellow inmate. The ABC said the Ombudsman also found that in 2009 the then acting commissioner of Corrections Victoria, Rod Wise, had emailed her saying there was little doubt Johnson was capable of harming Williams if he learned Williams was co-operating with police. Corrections Victoria nevertheless approved Williams's request to be housed with Johnson, a decision Justice Lasry called "breath-taking". Armytage's departure was announced in late June 2012; Premier Ted Baillieu said she would take a senior private-sector role.

Sir Ken Jones, who was Victoria Police's deputy commissioner when Williams died, told the royal commission into the management of police informants in 2019 that he believed compromised or corrupt prison staff were involved. In his statement he said the killing was pre-planned, and that "the plan involved corrupted and or compromised staff then serving within Corrections and criminal elements on the outside with much to lose if Williams was ever to give evidence". He added that he was "very surprised" the exercise bike had not been welded together. He also said the investigation into Williams's death was when he began to learn how deeply the barrister Nicola Gobbo had been used as a police informer; former commissioner Nixon told the same commission she was never told of Gobbo's role.

Roberta Williams, who was also a convicted drug dealer, later tried to profit from her notoriety. According to a 2022 Sydney Morning Herald column, she was bankrupt at the time of a 2019 reality-show plan, with debts of $405,759.17 against assets of $2,022.80, including $24,000 in school fees and $20,000 for her former husband's funeral. The columnist first met the couple in 2003. The same columnist wrote that after the producer Ryan Naumenko alleged he was beaten and threatened at a Collingwood studio, she and others were charged; the column says she pleaded guilty to blackmail and recklessly causing injury and received a two-year community corrections order, after a case that took more than three years.
